messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert Jensen, a 78-year-old database administrator, had a heart attack in his kitchen eighteen months ago. He remembers the crushing pressure in his chest, the cold sweat on his forehead, and the way the world narrowed to a single thought—this is it. The paramedics arrived, and as they worked on him, the sharp antiseptic smell of the ambulance hit his nostrils; that smell lodged itself somewhere deep. In the emergency room, he could taste the oxygen mask, hear the beeping, feel the hands pressing on his ribs. He survived, but his body had betrayed him. Now, whenever he recalls that morning—and he recalls it often—the same antiseptic odor floods his senses without warning, and the memory does not feel like a memory at all. It feels as real and immediate as the moment itself. He will be sitting at his desk, running database queries, and suddenly he is back in the stretcher, gasping, the world tilting. The reliving hits him with such force that he has to grip the arms of his chair to remind himself he is at home, that the attack is over. But his body does not believe that. His heart races, his palms sweat, and every twinge in his chest becomes a potential second act. He has come to see his own body as an enemy that remains on the offensive even when he is safe.

Robert lives alone now; his divorce predated the illness, but the heart attack deepened the isolation. He used to enjoy going to the office, chatting with colleagues over coffee. Now he works exclusively from home, and even there he feels on guard. He has checked his home’s smoke and carbon monoxide detectors four times this week. He paces from room to room, listening for any irregular sound. The hypervigilance has a relentless quality—he cannot sit still for more than a few minutes without scanning for signs of danger. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the fluorescent lights remind him of the hospital ceiling. He has not visited his primary care physician for a routine checkup in over a year; the thought of stepping into a waiting room sends him into a full-body panic. The world, he has concluded, is fundamentally dangerous. You can be healthy one minute and dying the next; there is no safety, no predictability. The faith he once had in life, in people, in the notion that he might have some control, has eroded completely. He feels a profound guilt, too, for not preventing the attack, for having ignored the early warning signs, and that guilt surfaces as tight-jawed anger at himself.

The consequences have accumulated quietly. Robert’s productivity has dropped by half. He cannot concentrate on work because he is constantly monitoring his heartbeat, waiting for the next flashback. His manager has noticed, and there have been conversations about performance targets that Robert dreads. He avoids video calls now because he is afraid his face will betray his terror. His daughter, who lives an hour away, has grown frustrated with his refusals to visit—he always says he is “not feeling well.” He knows she worries, but he cannot explain why he cannot leave his house. What would he say? That the world is a trap, that his own body is a ticking bomb? He has lost faith not only in the structure of his life but in the people who might help him; he is certain they will not understand the raw immediacy of his terror. Only last month, he smelled the antiseptic while brushing his teeth—some strange association with the mint—and he spent the next hour on the floor of his bathroom, trembling, the heart monitor on his watch flashing a red warning.

Robert finally came to the clinic because his daughter gave him an ultimatum: either see someone or she would stop calling. He is here, but he is skeptical. He is afraid that talking about the heart attack will make it come back, will make him relive it again. He is hoping, though, that someone can tell him why he cannot feel safe in his own living room, why his own body will not listen to reason, and perhaps—though he barely dares think it—why he feels so utterly alone in a world that keeps threatening to collapse.
